Coagulation I — The Cascade and Bleeding Disorders

How a clot is built, how the laboratory takes it apart one pathway at a time, and how to tell hemophilia from von Willebrand disease from a platelet defect at the bedside before a single assay is sent.

LectureCoagulation, Part 1
Objectives3 stated, 7 sections
SourcesSlides + recording
DateSept 4, 2026
Start here

How to use this file

Two Jobs, Held in Balance

The whole lecture rests on one idea stated on the first content slide: the coagulation system has to protect you from bleeding and protect you from clotting at the same time. Part 1 is what happens when the balance tips toward bleeding. Part 2 is the other direction.

Abbreviations used in this file PT prothrombin time — the clotting test for the extrinsic pathway · INR international normalised ratio — a standardised version of the PT so results compare across laboratories · aPTT activated partial thromboplastin time — the clotting test for the intrinsic pathway · VWF von Willebrand factor · VWD von Willebrand disease · F8 / FVIII factor 8 · F9 / FIX factor 9 · TF tissue factor, also called factor 3 · tPA tissue plasminogen activator · FDP fibrin degradation products · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · GPIb glycoprotein Ib — the platelet surface receptor that binds von Willebrand factor · HMWM high molecular weight multimers · DDAVP desmopressin · ADAMTS13 the enzyme that trims von Willebrand factor multimers · GI / GU gastrointestinal / genitourinary. A full glossary sits at the bottom of this file.
🔑 The four specifications of a working coagulation system

Worth learning as a list, because every disease in both coagulation lectures is a failure of exactly one of them:

  1. Balance protection from bleeding against protection from clotting Neither extreme is survivable.
  2. Maintain hemostasis and the patency of the circulatory system Seal holes without blocking the pipe.
  3. Respond to the site of injury quickly and in a localised fashion A clot must form fast, and only where the damage is. Systemic activation is disseminated intravascular coagulation, covered in objective 7.
  4. Return to the usual state once healing is complete This is fibrinolysis — the clot has to be dismantled again.
🧠 The three ingredients — and why the count is three, not one

Clotting needs platelets (right number and right function), a fibrin clot (correctly produced and correctly broken down), and blood vessels with healthy endothelium. Bleeding can come from a failure of any one of them, which is why the summary slide ends with the reminder that proper coagulation also depends on blood vessels and endothelium — a patient can bleed with a perfect coagulation panel.

Slide 6 — The three ingredients for clotting. Platelets, fibrin, and the vessel wall.

LO 1 — Cascade components

Objective 1

The Coagulation Cascade — Procoagulants, Anticoagulants, Fibrinolytics

Abbreviations in this section GPIb/IX/V glycoprotein Ib/IX/V — the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor · VWF von Willebrand factor · TF tissue factor, also called factor 3 · FXa, FVIIIa, FIIa activated factor 10, 8, 2 — a lower-case a means "activated" · tPA tissue plasminogen activator · FDP fibrin degradation products · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · Roman vs Arabic factor VIII = factor 8; both notations appear in the figures.

Hemostasis is taught in two stages that happen essentially at once. Primary hemostasis is the platelet plug. Secondary hemostasis is the fibrin mesh that reinforces it. Bleeding disorders sort cleanly along that seam, and objective 3 turns the seam into a bedside diagnostic.

🔑 Primary hemostasis — the platelet plug

Vessel injury exposes subendothelial collagen. Von Willebrand factor binds that collagen and unfurls, and the platelet receptor glycoprotein Ib/IX/V (GPIb/IX/V) binds the tethered von Willebrand factor. That is the adhesion step. Platelets then activate, release their granules, and aggregate to each other.

Hold on to that four-part chain — collagen → von Willebrand factor → GPIb → platelet — because two separate diseases break it at two different links, and the lecture puts them on one slide (objective 6).

Slide 7 — Primary hemostasis. Collagen tethers von Willebrand factor, which the platelet grips through GPIb/IX/V.

Slide 8 — Secondary hemostasis. The fibrin mesh that turns a fragile platelet plug into a stable clot.

🧠 Roman versus Arabic numerals — a deliberate note from the lecture

The factors are traditionally written in Roman numerals (factor VIII), and the lecturer numbers them in Arabic (factor 8) throughout. Both appear in the figures, so read them interchangeably: II = 2, V = 5, VII = 7, VIII = 8, IX = 9, X = 10, XI = 11, XII = 12, XIII = 13. An activated factor carries a lower-case a — FXa is activated factor 10.

🎙️ Why factors 3, 4 and 6 are missing from the list

A question the numbered list always raises. The gaps are historical, not an oversight:

  • Factor 3 is tissue factor. Nobody calls it factor 3 any more.
  • Factor 4 is calcium. Identified early as a required "factor", then recognised as simply an ion.
  • Factor 6 was retired — what had been numbered separately turned out to be an already-numbered factor in its activated form, so the number was dropped rather than reused.

And the practical consequence of calcium being "factor 4": a patient who is hypocalcemic has a problem with clotting. That is worth carrying into massive transfusion (where citrated blood chelates the patient's calcium) and into DiGeorge syndrome, where hypocalcemia is part of the phenotype.

Slide 9 — The waterfall cascade. Note the dotted green lines: thrombin (FIIa) feeds back and amplifies its own production.

🎙️ Roman versus Arabic numerals — a stated source of real error

The lecture is blunt about this: the Roman numbering is historical, almost nobody uses Roman numerals in daily life any more, and that causes genuine errors when reading a cascade diagram. The aside offered as a memory aid — outside coagulation, about the only place most people still meet Roman numerals is the Super Bowl.

So read both fluently, and be deliberate about it: II = 2, V = 5, VII = 7, VIII = 8, IX = 9, X = 10, XI = 11, XII = 12, XIII = 13. The pairs that actually get mixed up are VII (7) versus VIII (8) — extrinsic versus intrinsic, and PT versus aPTT — and XI (11) versus XII (12), where one causes bleeding and one does not.

🪝 Memory hook — read the cascade diagram as two arms joining one trunk

The left arm starts at a negatively charged surface and runs 12 → 11 → 9 → 8 — the intrinsic pathway, measured by the aPTT. The right arm starts at tissue factor exposure and is just 7 — the extrinsic pathway, measured by the PT. They meet at factor 10 and run down the shared trunk 10 → 5 → 2 (prothrombin → thrombin) → fibrinogen → fibrin — the common pathway, which moves both tests. Factor 13 then cross-links the fibrin.

The dotted feed-forward arrows are the part people skip: thrombin activates factors 5, 8, 11 and 13. It accelerates its own production, which is what makes the response fast enough to be useful.

🎙️ Where the coagulation proteins are actually made — and the one exception

Stated in the recording and not on the slides, but it is the fact that makes liver disease and von Willebrand disease behave the way they do:

The liver makes all of the coagulation factors except von Willebrand factor and factor 8.

  • Von Willebrand factor comes from endothelial cells (Weibel–Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes.
  • Factor 8 is largely endothelial in origin and is carried in plasma bound to von Willebrand factor.

Two payoffs. In liver disease everything falls except these two, so factor 8 is characteristically normal or even high — which is one way to separate liver disease from disseminated intravascular coagulation, where factor 8 is consumed along with everything else. And it is why the endothelium, not the hepatocyte, is the organ of interest in von Willebrand disease.

The anticoagulants — what keeps the clot local

🧠 The natural brakes
  • Protein C and protein S — together they inactivate factors 5a and 8a. Two of the most important thrombophilias in Part 2 are deficiencies of these.
  • Antithrombin III — neutralises thrombin and factor 10a. This is the protein heparin works through, which is why antithrombin deficiency makes heparin less effective.
  • Plasmin — the enzyme that digests fibrin.
  • Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) — converts plasminogen to plasmin.
  • Intact endothelial surface — expresses heparans, so a healthy vessel lining is actively anticoagulant rather than merely neutral.
⚠️ A naming trap that costs marks

Protein C and protein S are anticoagulants. Factor 5 and factor 8 are procoagulants. Because protein C inactivates factor 5, a mutation that makes factor 5 resistant to protein C (factor V Leiden) produces the same net effect as losing protein C — more clotting. That equivalence is stated explicitly in Part 2 and is a favourite question stem.

🎙️ Two asides on the anticoagulant list
  • Heparans (with an "a") on the endothelium are the natural relatives of heparin (with an "i"), the drug. The intact vessel lining is therefore actively anticoagulant, and heparin therapy is essentially borrowing a mechanism the endothelium already uses.
  • Tissue plasminogen activator is the "clot-busting drug" given in acute stroke. Given at the site of a clot it generates plasmin locally and dissolves it — the therapeutic use of the same pathway described here as normal physiology.

The mirror image is also worth knowing: too much antiplasmin, or overexpression of the fibrinolysis inhibitors, causes a clotting problem, because clots are not taken down when they should be. Rare, but it completes the logic.

Fibrinolysis — taking the clot apart

The fourth specification from the orientation. Once healing is complete the clot has to go, and vessel patency has to be restored. tPA converts plasminogen to plasmin; plasmin digests fibrin into fibrin degradation products, of which the measurable one is the D-dimer.

Slide 12 — Fibrinolysis. The end of the cascade: how the clot is dissolved and vessel patency restored.

🎙️ Where the name "D-dimer" comes from

Fibrin monomers contain regions labelled D and E. When factor 13 cross-links fibrin it locks two adjacent D regions together. Plasmin then cuts the mesh up, but it cannot break that cross-link — so the fragment released carries two D regions: a D-dimer.

That is exactly why the test means what it means. A D-dimer can only exist if fibrin was formed, cross-linked by factor 13, and then broken down. It is a marker of clot turnover, not merely of clotting.

🔑 Why the D-dimer matters clinically

A D-dimer is a fragment released when cross-linked fibrin is broken down — so a raised D-dimer means a clot was formed and is being degraded. It appears again in Part 2 as part of the workup for thrombosis, and in objective 7 of this file as one of the four laboratory legs of disseminated intravascular coagulation.

🎙️ Why factor 13 is drawn off to the side of the cascade

On most cascade diagrams factor 13 sits apart from the main chain, and the recording explains why: it acts on the fibrin clot after the clot has already formed. It triggers a change in the clot's configuration so that the finished mesh is stronger.

That placement is the clinical picture. Patients with factor 13 deficiency do make a clot — so the PT, the aPTT and the platelet count are all normal, because every one of those stops at the point the first fibrin appears. The clot is simply not as strong as it should be, and it falls off sooner than it should. Hence delayed bleeding, and, added in the recording, delayed wound healing.

Q: A patient has an isolated prolonged aPTT with a completely normal PT. Which factors could be responsible, and which single one of them will not cause bleeding?

Answer

An isolated prolonged aPTT points at the intrinsic pathway: factors 8, 9, 11 and 12. If a common-pathway factor (2, 5, 10) or fibrinogen were low, the PT would be prolonged too.

The exception is factor 12 deficiency, which prolongs the aPTT but does not cause bleeding — stated directly on the aPTT slide. It is an in-vitro artefact of the contact-activation reagent rather than a real hemostatic defect, and it is the classic distractor when a question gives you a long aPTT in an asymptomatic patient found on pre-operative screening.

The mechanism, from the recording: in vivo you do not need factor 12 at all — there is a backup contact system using other contact factors. The in vitro test, however, genuinely depends on factor 12 being present. It is a case where the assay is not the same as the body. It still matters to make the diagnosis, because otherwise every aPTT this patient ever has will come back abnormal and be re-investigated.

Q: Von Willebrand factor has two jobs. Name both, and explain why a patient with severe von Willebrand disease can have a prolonged aPTT.

Answer

(1) It mediates platelet adhesion — it binds exposed subendothelial collagen and is then gripped by the platelet receptor GPIb. (2) It is the carrier protein for factor 8, binding it and prolonging its half-life.

Because of job (2), losing von Willebrand factor means factor 8 is cleared faster and its level falls. Factor 8 is an intrinsic-pathway factor, so a secondary factor 8 deficiency prolongs the aPTT. This is why severe (type 3) von Willebrand disease can look like mild hemophilia A on a coagulation screen — and why the two must be separated with von Willebrand antigen and activity assays, not the aPTT.

LO 2 — Pathways and their tests

Objective 2

PT, INR, aPTT and the Mixing Study

Two clotting times and one follow-up test carry most of the diagnostic weight. The trick is that the pattern of which test is prolonged tells you which arm of the cascade is broken, and the mixing study then tells you whether something is missing or something is blocking.

Abbreviations in this section PT prothrombin time · INR international normalised ratio · aPTT activated partial thromboplastin time · TT thrombin time · FDP fibrin degradation products · TEG / ROTEM thromboelastography / thromboelastometry — viscoelastic tests that watch a clot form and dissolve in real time · K3 / K2 EDTA potassium salts of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, the anticoagulant in a lavender-top tube.
⚠️ Before any of this: the collection tube

Coagulation samples go into sodium citrate tubes — the light blue top. Citrate reversibly chelates calcium, so the laboratory can add calcium back and start the reaction on demand. (Contrast with the lavender-top EDTA tube used for the complete blood count, where the calcium binding is not reversed.)

The critical detail: the ratio of whole blood to anticoagulant must be 9:1. An underfilled tube carries proportionally too much citrate, so when calcium is added back there is not enough of it — producing an artificially prolonged clotting time. Such samples are rejected by the laboratory. A short-draw blue top is one of the most common reasons a "coagulopathy" turns out not to exist.

Slide 15 — Which test covers which pathway. The common pathway sits under both.

TestPathway measuredFactors it is sensitive toProlonged by

aPTTIntrinsic + commonMost sensitive to factors 8, 9, 11, 12Hemophilia A and B, heparin, lupus anticoagulant, factor 12 deficiency
Both PT and aPTTCommonFactors 2, 5, 10 and fibrinogenLiver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation, common-pathway factor deficiency
D-dimer, FDPFibrinolysis—Any active clot formation and breakdown — thrombosis, DIC

Slide 16 — PT. Most sensitive to factor 7.

Slide 17 — aPTT. Most sensitive to factors 8, 9, 11, 12.

🎙️ What the analyzer physically does — and why this test cannot see platelets
  1. Spin the citrate tube and take the plasma onlyThe cells, including every platelet, are discarded with the pellet.
  2. Load the plasma; the instrument adds calcium backReversing the citrate and restoring clotting capability.
  3. Add the activatorThromboplastin for the PT, partial thromboplastin for the aPTT.
  4. Time until a clot forms, in secondsA longer time means a factor is missing.

Step 1 is the whole explanation of the blind spot. These are plasma assays. The platelets were removed before the test began, so the PT and aPTT are structurally incapable of detecting a platelet problem — and von Willebrand factor's platelet-tethering role is invisible to them for the same reason. This is not a sensitivity limitation that a better reagent could fix.

🔑 The 50% rule — and why a slightly long clotting time may mean nothing

Factor levels of roughly 50% are enough for hemostasis. That single number explains three separate things on the slides:

  • A clotting time only prolongs once a factor drops well below normal — so slight prolongation may not indicate bleeding risk at all.
  • Sensitivity and specificity vary with the reagent the laboratory uses, so the exact threshold is not universal.
  • It is also why the mixing study works: adding an equal volume of normal plasma lifts a deficient patient to about 50%, which is enough to correct the time.
🎙️ The actual numbers behind the "50% rule"

The recording puts figures on the curve, which makes the rule far more usable:

Factor levelWhat the clotting time doesWhat it means for the patient
~50%aPTT just begins to prolong (PT at around 55%)Flags as abnormal on the report
30–40%Mildly prolonged"You are probably okay" — no spontaneous bleeding
<20%aPTT above ~45 secondsThis is hemophilia territory
<1% (severe)aPTT over 100 secondsSpontaneous bleeding

And the reason a marginally abnormal result may mean nothing at all: a reference range is built by running healthy volunteers and taking the 95% confidence interval. By construction, about 5% of perfectly healthy people fall outside it. A value a little past the line may simply be a normal person, not a diagnosis.

⚠️ The blind spot — a normal PT and aPTT does not exclude a bleeding disorder

Stated explicitly on the slides and worth over-learning: von Willebrand disease and platelet function disorders do not significantly affect the PT or aPTT. Both are diseases of primary hemostasis, and neither clotting time looks at platelets at all. A patient with a lifetime of nosebleeds, heavy periods and easy bruising can have a perfectly normal coagulation screen. Ordering a PT and aPTT and stopping there is how von Willebrand disease gets missed for decades.

Slide 18 — Prolonged clotting times. Around 50% of normal factor level is enough for hemostasis.

The mixing study — missing, or blocked?

A clotting time is long. There are only two explanations: the patient is missing a factor, or the patient has an inhibitor — something in the plasma actively interfering. The mixing study separates them in one step.

  1. Mix patient plasma with normal pooled plasma Usually 1:1. This supplies every factor at roughly half the normal concentration.
  2. Repeat the clotting time Then read the result against the 50% rule.
  3. It corrects → factor deficiency The donated factors were enough to restore clotting, so the patient was simply short of something.
  4. It does not correct → inhibitor Something in the patient's plasma is neutralising the added factors too. Examples: an acquired factor 8 antibody, or a lupus anticoagulant.

Slide 19 — The mixing study. Corrects means deficiency; fails to correct means inhibitor.

🎙️ The incubated mixing study — catching a slow inhibitor

An important refinement not on the slides. Some inhibitors — classically the acquired factor 8 antibody — are slow-acting. On an immediate 1:1 mix they appear to correct, because the antibody has not had time to neutralise the added factor.

The fix is to incubate the mix at 37 °C for 30–60 minutes and re-time it. If the clotting time drifts back out on incubation, the antibody has been slowly destroying the donated factor 8 — an inhibitor, despite the reassuring immediate result.

An immediate mix that corrects does not by itself exclude an inhibitor. If the clinical picture is a new bleeding diathesis, ask for the incubated study.

🪝 Memory hook — "corrects = missing, stays long = blocked"

Deficiency is a subtraction problem, so adding plasma fixes it. An inhibitor is an opposition problem, so adding plasma just gives the inhibitor more to attack. The same test reappears in Part 2 as the front end of the lupus anticoagulant workup — there, the extra twist is that the clotting time also corrects with added phospholipid, which is what proves the inhibitor is directed at phospholipid rather than at a factor.

Q: A blue-top tube arrives half-filled. The aPTT comes back markedly prolonged in a patient with no bleeding history. What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen next?

Answer

A pre-analytic artefact from an underfilled citrate tube. The 9:1 whole-blood to citrate ratio is broken, so there is excess citrate relative to blood. When the laboratory recalcifies the sample, that excess citrate soaks up the added calcium and the clotting time comes out artificially prolonged.

The sample should be rejected and redrawn, properly filled. This is a laboratory-error question, not a hematology question, and it is exactly the kind of thing a hematology/coagulation laboratory director puts on a test.

Q: Both PT and aPTT are prolonged. A 1:1 mix with normal plasma corrects neither. Give two categories of cause.

Answer

Failure to correct means an inhibitor, and involvement of both tests points at the common pathway or at something non-specific:

  • A specific factor inhibitor against a common-pathway factor — for example an acquired antibody to factor 5.
  • A non-specific inhibitor, classically a lupus anticoagulant, or an interfering substance such as heparin contamination from a line draw, or a paraprotein.

Remember the paradox carried into Part 2: a lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting in vitro but increases thrombosis risk in vivo.

Q: A 68-year-old with new spontaneous bruising has an aPTT of 62 seconds. A 1:1 mix with normal plasma corrects to 34 seconds. The team concludes there is no inhibitor. What have they missed?

Answer

They have missed a slow-acting inhibitor, and they need an incubated mixing study.

Acquired factor 8 antibodies are time- and temperature-dependent. On an immediate mix the antibody has not yet had time to neutralise the donated factor 8, so the clotting time corrects and looks like a simple deficiency. Incubating the mix at 37 °C for 30–60 minutes and re-timing it lets the antibody act, and the aPTT drifts back out.

The clinical setting should have prompted this from the start: a new bleeding diathesis in an older patient with no lifetime history is acquired hemophilia A until proven otherwise. Confirm with a factor 8 level and a Bethesda titre, and treat with a bypassing agent plus immunosuppression to eradicate the antibody.

Q: A patient's aPTT comes back at 41 seconds against a reference range of 25–39. They have never bled, including through two prior operations. How worried should you be?

Answer

Barely at all. Two separate reasons converge:

  • A reference range is the 95% confidence interval of healthy volunteers, so roughly 5% of entirely normal people sit outside it by construction. A value a whisker past the line is often just a normal person.
  • The factor-level curve only begins to prolong the aPTT at around 50%, and a level of 30–40% is still hemostatically adequate. Meaningful hemophilia sits below 20%, with an aPTT above about 45 seconds; severe disease runs over 100 seconds.

The negative bleeding history through prior surgery is the strongest single piece of evidence. If anything is pursued, the likeliest finding is factor 12 deficiency — a prolonged aPTT with no bleeding risk, worth documenting so the result is not re-investigated every admission.

LO 3 — Distinguishing conditions

Objective 3 · part 1

Reading a Bleeding Pattern Before You Order Anything

Abbreviations in this section GI / GU gastrointestinal / genitourinary · Petechiae pinpoint non-blanching skin haemorrhages · Ecchymosis a bruise · Hemarthrosis bleeding into a joint · Epistaxis nosebleed · Menorrhagia heavy menstrual bleeding · VWD von Willebrand disease · Antiplasmin the natural inhibitor of plasmin · Kasabach–Merritt a vascular tumour that consumes platelets inside itself.

The single highest-yield idea in this lecture is that where a patient bleeds tells you which half of hemostasis has failed. The lecture makes this a matching exercise on one slide, and the answer is worth memorising cold.

🔑 The match game — three bleeding patterns, three disease families
Bleeding patternDisease familyWhich half of hemostasis
Mucocutaneous bleeding — nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, bruisingvon Willebrand disease (and platelet disorders)Primary — the platelet plug
Joint and muscle bleeding — hemarthrosis, deep hematomaHemophilia A or B (factor 8 or factor 9 deficiency)Secondary — the fibrin mesh
Delayed bleeding — stops, then restarts hours laterFactor 13 deficiency or antiplasmin deficiencyClot stabilisation / fibrinolysis
🪝 Memory hook — surfaces, spaces, and the second act

Platelets patch surfaces, so when platelets fail you bleed from surfaces — skin and mucosa. Fibrin fills spaces, so when fibrin fails you bleed into spaces — joints and muscles. Factor 13 cross-links the finished clot, so when it fails the initial plug forms normally and then falls apart — bleeding that is delayed, not immediate. Delayed bleeding after circumcision or a dental extraction with a normal PT, aPTT and platelet count is the classic factor 13 stem, because factor 13 deficiency does not prolong either clotting time.

Slide 24 — Clinical assessment of bleeding. Platelet defects on the left, coagulation disorders on the right.

Bleeding symptomPlatelet defects (primary hemostasis)Coagulation disorders (secondary hemostasis)
General patternMucocutaneous — oral cavity, nasal, gastrointestinal, genitourinaryDeep tissue — joints and muscles
Excessive bleeding after minor cutsYesNot usually
PetechiaeCommonUncommon

Hemarthroses, muscle hematomasUncommonCommon in severe deficiency, or with injury in mild/moderate deficiency

🎙️ The lecturer's own expansion of the three patterns

Asked to fill in the match game live, the answers came with detail worth keeping:

  • Hemophilia — joint bleeding, deep muscle bleeding, and retroperitoneal bleeding. And the long-term consequence: joint arthropathy is a major cause of morbidity — repeated bleeds into a joint cause scarring, and the joint progressively stops working. That is what prophylaxis exists to prevent.
  • von Willebrand disease — mucocutaneous: heavy periods, gum bleeding, purpura.
  • Factor 13 — delayed bleeding and delayed wound healing.

With one honest caveat: "it is never as clear-cut as you only get one type." These are the predominant patterns, not exclusive ones — and if any of these patients goes to surgery, all of them bleed. The pattern is a pointer for the undifferentiated patient, not a rule.

The full differential of bleeding

Factor problems

Deficiency of, or inhibitors to, factors 8 and 9 (hemophilia A and B) or factors 2, 5, 7, 10, 11.

Fibrinogen problems

Afibrinogenemia (none), hypofibrinogenemia (too little), dysfibrinogenemia (present but non-functional — and this one can cause clotting as well as bleeding).

Clot stabilisation

Factor 13 or antiplasmin deficiency — delayed bleeding with normal screening tests.

Platelet problems

Thrombocytopenia (too few) or platelet function defects (enough, but they do not work).

Von Willebrand disease

The most common inherited bleeding disorder. Gets its own objective below.

Not the coagulation system at all

Vessel and connective-tissue causes — see the callout below. A normal coagulation panel does not end the workup.

🧠 Bleeding that has nothing to do with clotting factors

A separate slide lists these deliberately, because the coagulation panel will be normal in all of them:

  • Structural malformations — hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia; Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon, where a fast-growing vascular tumour consumes platelets inside itself.
  • Connective tissue disorders, hereditary or acquired — for example Ehlers–Danlos syndrome. The vessel wall has no support.
  • Small vessel vasculitis.
  • Paraproteins — abnormal immunoglobulins that interfere with platelets and fibrin.
  • Skin diseases, infections, psychogenic causes.
  • Trauma and surgery — the commonest cause of bleeding overall, and the one that gets forgotten in a hematology lecture.

Q: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with a swollen, painful, warm knee after a minor fall. There is no history of nosebleeds. Which half of hemostasis is failing, and what should the coagulation screen show?

Answer

Secondary hemostasis. Hemarthrosis — bleeding into a joint — is the signature of a coagulation factor deficiency, not a platelet problem, and the absence of mucocutaneous bleeding supports that. In a boy this age the answer is hemophilia A or B until proven otherwise.

Expect a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT (factors 8 and 9 are both intrinsic), a normal platelet count, and a mixing study that corrects — because this is a deficiency, not an inhibitor. Factor 8 and factor 9 activity assays then separate hemophilia A from B.

Q: A teenager bleeds normally at the time of a dental extraction, goes home, and starts bleeding again 18 hours later. PT, aPTT and platelet count are all normal. What are you thinking of?

Answer

Factor 13 deficiency (or antiplasmin deficiency). The pattern is delayed bleeding: the platelet plug and the initial fibrin mesh form normally, so the immediate hemostasis is fine — but factor 13 cross-links fibrin, and without it the clot is not stabilised and later breaks down.

The critical point is that factor 13 deficiency is invisible to the PT and aPTT, both of which stop timing the moment the first fibrin strands appear. It needs a specific factor 13 assay (classically a clot solubility test). Delayed bleeding with a normal screen is the whole question.

Q: An isolated prolonged aPTT can come from factors 8, 9, 11 or 12. Rank those four by what they mean for the patient.

Answer
  • Factor 8 — hemophilia A. X-linked, 1 in 5,000 males, the most common. Joint and muscle bleeding.
  • Factor 9 — hemophilia B. X-linked, 1 in 30,000 males. Clinically indistinguishable from A; only a factor assay separates them.
  • Factor 11 — hemophilia C. Autosomal, so it affects both sexes. Bleeding is typically milder and correlates poorly with the factor level, often surfacing only after surgery or trauma.
  • Factor 12 — no bleeding at all. It prolongs the aPTT because the in vitro contact-activation reagent needs it, but in vivo there is a backup contact system, so the patient is hemostatically normal.

The clean summary: 8 and 9 bleed severely, 11 bleeds mildly, 12 does not bleed.

🎮Where Are They Bleeding?

0 / 0

A bleeding presentation at a time. Sort it into primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, or clot stabilisation.

LO 3 — Hemophilia

Objective 3 · part 2

Hemophilia A and B

Two diseases, one phenotype. Factor 8 deficiency and factor 9 deficiency are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside — both are X-linked, both cause joint and muscle bleeding, both prolong the aPTT alone. Only a factor assay separates them.

Abbreviations in this section F8 / FVIII factor 8 — deficient in hemophilia A · F9 / FIX factor 9 — deficient in hemophilia B, also called Christmas disease · Inhibitor an alloantibody the patient develops against infused factor, which neutralises it.
Hemophilia AHemophilia B
Missing factorFactor 8Factor 9
InheritanceX-linked — so it presents in males, carried by females
Incidence1 in 5,000 males1 in 30,000 males — six times rarer
Coagulation screenProlonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count; mixing study corrects
Bleeding patternJoint (hemarthrosis) and muscle bleeding — deep tissue, not mucocutaneous
🎙️ Hemophilia C — the third one, not on the slides

Stated explicitly in the recording: the intrinsic-pathway factors 8, 9 and 11 are all associated with a hemophilia.

NameFactorInheritanceNote
Hemophilia AFactor 8X-linkedThe most common
Hemophilia BFactor 9X-linkedChristmas disease
Hemophilia CFactor 11AutosomalAffects both sexes; enriched in Ashkenazi Jewish populations. Bleeding is typically milder and poorly correlated with the factor level, often only after surgery or trauma

Hemophilia C is the reason to say "factors 8, 9, 11 and 12" when listing what prolongs an isolated aPTT, and then to remember that 11 bleeds and 12 does not.

🔑 Severity is defined by the factor level, not by the symptoms
Factor level (% of normal)SeverityWhat it means clinically
< 1%SevereSpontaneous bleeding, including into joints, with no identifiable trauma
1–5%ModerateBleeding with minor trauma
>5–30%MildBleeding usually only with surgery or significant trauma

Line this up against the 50% rule from objective 2: a factor level of 30% is below the level needed for full hemostasis but well above the severe range — which is why mild hemophilia can go undiagnosed until a first operation.

Slide 25 — Hemophilia. X-linked inheritance, famously through the European royal families.

🎙️ The treatment target, and why these patients no longer receive plasma

The goal is not a normal factor level. The recording is specific: keeping a patient above roughly 20–30% is good, and above 5% already sharply reduces spontaneous bleeding — which is what drives the joint damage. Higher targets, sustained for longer, are used around major surgery.

And a piece of history that explains current practice. In the 1980s, patients with hemophilia began developing AIDS with no sexual risk factors, and that observation is one of the ways HIV transmission through blood was established — because these patients were receiving chronic plasma transfusions as their source of factor 8 and factor 9.

Modern pharmaceutical factor concentrates undergo viral inactivation, giving essentially zero viral transmission risk. So the rule that follows is now firm: patients with hemophilia should not receive plasma or cryoprecipitate — only as an absolute last resort when no concentrate is available. This is the same reasoning behind the "avoid cryoprecipitate" instruction in von Willebrand disease.

Therapy — and the complication that dominates management

  • Coagulation factor concentrates are the mainstay, given both as prophylaxis and as treatment of bleeds. Prophylaxis, not on-demand treatment, is what preserves joints.
  • Inhibitors — antibodies against the infused factor — cause big problems. Once a patient develops one, the factor they are given is neutralised and ordinary replacement stops working. This is the single biggest management problem in hemophilia.
  • Emicizumab (Hemlibra) is a bypassing agent. It is a bispecific antibody that bridges factor 9a and factor 10 — physically doing the job that factor 8a normally does as a cofactor. Because it is not factor 8, an anti-factor-8 inhibitor cannot neutralise it, which is exactly why it works in inhibitor patients.

Slide 26 — Emicizumab (Hemlibra). A bispecific antibody that substitutes for factor 8a by bridging factor 9a to factor 10.

🪝 Memory hook — emicizumab is a molecular clamp, not a replacement

Factor 8a does not cut anything — it is a cofactor that holds factor 9a and factor 10 next to each other so the reaction can happen. Emicizumab has two arms: one grabs factor 9a, the other grabs factor 10. It reproduces the geometry without reproducing the protein. That is what makes it invisible to an anti-factor-8 antibody, and why a patient on it will have an aPTT that looks falsely normal or short — a known trap when interpreting coagulation tests in these patients.

Q: A boy with severe hemophilia A has been well controlled on factor 8 concentrate but now bleeds through his usual dose. What has most likely happened, and what class of agent addresses it?

Answer

He has developed an inhibitor — an alloantibody against factor 8 that neutralises the infused product. The clue is loss of response to a dose that previously worked. This is confirmed on a mixing study that fails to correct (an inhibitor pattern), and quantified with a Bethesda titre.

The answer is a bypassing agent — in current practice emicizumab (Hemlibra), which restores factor 8a's bridging function between factor 9a and factor 10 using a molecule the anti-factor-8 antibody does not recognise.

Q: Why does hemophilia present in boys, and how can a girl be affected?

Answer

Both factor 8 and factor 9 genes are on the X chromosome. A male has only one X, so a single defective copy leaves him with no normal allele — hence 1 in 5,000 males for hemophilia A and 1 in 30,000 males for B.

A female with one affected X is usually a carrier, but can bleed through skewed (unfavourable) X-inactivation — if the normal X is preferentially silenced, her factor level can fall into the symptomatic range. Less commonly, she can be affected by homozygosity (affected father and carrier mother) or by Turner syndrome, where a single X is present.

LO 3 — von Willebrand disease

Objective 3 · part 3

von Willebrand Disease — The Common One

The most common inherited bleeding disorder, and the one most likely to be sitting undiagnosed in a clinic. It is also the one the routine coagulation screen misses, which is why the diagnosis rests on a specific set of assays.

Abbreviations in this section VWF von Willebrand factor · VWD von Willebrand disease · VWF:Ag von Willebrand factor antigen — how much protein is present · VWF:RCo ristocetin cofactor activity — how well that protein works · HMWM high molecular weight multimers — the largest, most hemostatically active forms · DDAVP desmopressin — a vasopressin analogue that releases stored von Willebrand factor · GPIb platelet glycoprotein Ib receptor.

How common

~1% of people have asymptomatic von Willebrand factor abnormalities; ~1 in 8,000 have symptomatic disease.

Inheritance

Most often autosomal dominant — note the contrast with X-linked hemophilia. It affects both sexes.

Named for

Erik von Willebrand (1870–1949), Finnish physician.

Presentation

Bruising and mucosal bleeding — epistaxis, menorrhagia, gingival bleeding; also soft-tissue hematomas and surgical or traumatic bleeding.

🧠 The protein — and why its size is the whole story

Von Willebrand factor is a large multimeric glycoprotein made by endothelial cells (stored in Weibel–Palade bodies) and by megakaryocytes. It is made as a propolypeptide; the propeptide is cleaved off and the remaining protein polymerises into high molecular weight multimers.

Those big multimers are the functional ones. Hemostatic activity tracks molecular weight — ultra-large and high multimers do most of the work; low multimers do least. The enzyme ADAMTS13 trims them down to size, and in Part 2 the failure of that trimming causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Same molecule, opposite disease.

Two jobs: (1) bind platelet GPIb and mediate adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen; (2) act as the carrier for factor 8, binding it and prolonging its half-life.

Slide 28 — Von Willebrand factor. A large multimer that both grips collagen and carries factor 8.

🎙️ Erik von Willebrand and the Åland islands

Von Willebrand described the disease in families from the islands of the Baltic Sea — the Åland archipelago — where a profound bleeding tendency ran through related families. The detail the recording lingers on: some of the teenage girls died of blood loss from heavy menstrual bleeding.

It is worth holding onto, because menorrhagia is still the most commonly missed presentation. Heavy periods get normalised for years before anyone sends a von Willebrand panel — and the routine coagulation screen, as above, will be entirely normal.

The two assays that make the diagnosis

🔑 Ristocetin cofactor assay — measuring function
  1. Normal fixed plateletsSupplied by the laboratory, so the platelets are never the variable.
  2. Add patient plasmaThis supplies the patient's von Willebrand factor.
  3. Add ristocetinAn antibiotic that artificially induces von Willebrand factor to bind GPIb — it forces the adhesion reaction to happen in a tube.
  4. Measure agglutination as increased light transmissionClumped platelets let more light through. Agglutination is proportional to von Willebrand factor activity.

Slide 29 — Ristocetin cofactor assay. Ristocetin forces VWF onto GPIb; agglutination is read as light transmission.

🎙️ Why the assay uses ristocetin — an antibiotic that was withdrawn

Ristocetin was developed as an antibiotic. Patients taking it started turning up with bruising; their platelet counts were falling, and they were bleeding. The cause was eventually traced to the fact that ristocetin activates von Willebrand factor, driving it onto platelets and clearing them from the circulation.

Nobody takes ristocetin as an antibiotic any more — but the laboratory kept it, precisely because that side effect is a controllable, quantifiable trigger of the GPIb interaction. The drug's failure is the assay's mechanism.

Two practical notes from the recording: the antigen is measured by a standard ELISA, and multimer analysis is not a front-line test — it is sent after the activity-to-antigen comparison has already shown something is wrong.

🔑 Multimer analysis — measuring size distribution

A Western blot: separate the multimeric forms by electrophoresis, transfer to a solid support, and detect with an antibody to von Willebrand factor. Three possible results:

  • Normal pattern — full ladder of multimers present.
  • Abnormal pattern — usually loss of the high molecular weight forms. This is the qualitative defect.
  • Essentially absent — almost no von Willebrand factor at all.

Slide 30 — Multimer analysis. Hemostatic activity runs with molecular weight; ADAMTS13 does the trimming.

🎙️ Reading the multimer gel, and why size is the whole point

The gel is loaded at the top. The ultra-large and high molecular weight multimers are too bulky to navigate the gel, so they stay near the origin; the smaller forms migrate further down. A normal lane shows the full ladder — low, intermediate, high and ultra-large.

And the reason losing the big ones matters, put physically: von Willebrand factor has to stretch from the collagen at the injury site out into the flowing blood to catch a passing platelet. A short multimer cannot span that distance. So a patient who makes only the small forms has plenty of von Willebrand factor antigen and still bleeds — which is exactly the type 2 pattern: normal antigen, low activity, abnormal multimers.

Classification — one question decides everything

🪝 The diagnostic algorithm in one sentence

Are activity and antigen similar? If yes, the protein present works normally — there is just not enough of it: a quantitative problem, types 1 and 3. If no — antigen is much higher than activity — the protein is present but broken: a qualitative problem, type 2.

TypeProblemVon Willebrand factor levelActivity : antigen ratioMultimers
Type 1Quantitative — partial deficiency. The most common form.Decreased, <30%Similar — roughly normal ratioNormal pattern, reduced amount
Type 2 (2A, 2B, 2M, 2N)Qualitative — the protein is abnormalMay be near-normalReduced, < ~0.5–0.7Abnormal pattern — usually loss of high molecular weight forms
Type 3Quantitative — essentially complete absence. The severe form.Essentially absent, <3%Both near zeroEssentially absent
⚠️ Two grey zones the lecture flags explicitly
  • "Low von Willebrand factor" of 30–50% sits between normal and type 1. It may be von Willebrand disease if there is a bleeding history — the clinical history, not the number alone, decides.
  • Blood group O individuals have lower von Willebrand factor levels at baseline. A group O patient can test in the low range and be entirely normal. Interpret the level against the patient's blood type, or you will over-diagnose.
🎙️ Desmopressin in practice — and the trial that precedes it
  • It is available as a nasal spray as well as parenterally, so a patient can take it themselves before a planned challenge — surgery, a dental procedure, a period.
  • It releases both von Willebrand factor and factor 8 from endothelial stores. Target: lift the level above roughly 30–40%.
  • Response is tested before it is relied upon. The DDAVP trial: draw a baseline von Willebrand level, give the desmopressin, then draw serial levels afterwards and plot the response curve. A patient who does not respond is identified before the operation, not during it, and is given concentrate instead.

Therapy — matched to the type

TypeFirst-line treatmentWhy
Type 1Desmopressin (DDAVP)Releases stored von Willebrand factor from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies. Works because the stored protein is normal — there is simply more of it available on demand.
Types 2A, 2MDDAVP may work if there is some residual activity; otherwise plasma-derived factor 8 concentrates (Humate P, Alphanate)Releasing more of an abnormal protein only helps if the protein partly works.
Types 2B, 3Humate P, Alphanate — concentrate, not DDAVPType 3 has nothing stored to release. In type 2B the abnormal von Willebrand factor binds platelets too avidly, so releasing more can worsen thrombocytopenia.
Also available: plasma-derived von Willebrand factor (Wilate) or recombinant von Willebrand factor (Vonvendi). Avoid exposing patients to cryoprecipitate — it carries an unnecessary infectious-exposure risk when virally-inactivated concentrates exist.

Q: A woman with lifelong heavy periods and easy bruising has a normal PT, aPTT and platelet count. Von Willebrand antigen is 60%, ristocetin cofactor activity is 22%. Which type of von Willebrand disease is this, and should she be given desmopressin?

Answer

Type 2 — a qualitative defect. The activity-to-antigen ratio is 22/60 = 0.37, well under the 0.5–0.7 threshold, meaning plenty of protein is present but it does not work. A type 1 patient would have activity and antigen falling together. Multimer analysis is the next test, and would be expected to show loss of high molecular weight multimers.

Not desmopressin as a reflex. In types 2A and 2M it may help if there is residual activity; in type 2B it can make things worse by driving abnormal von Willebrand factor onto platelets and deepening the thrombocytopenia. The subtype must be established first — if it cannot be, use a plasma-derived factor 8 / von Willebrand factor concentrate.

Q: Why does von Willebrand disease cause mucocutaneous bleeding, when hemophilia — also a "clotting protein" problem — causes joint bleeding?

Answer

Because von Willebrand factor's dominant role is in primary hemostasis. It is the tether between subendothelial collagen and the platelet receptor GPIb, so losing it is functionally a platelet adhesion defect — and platelet problems bleed from surfaces: nose, gums, uterus, gut.

Hemophilia is a defect of secondary hemostasis — the fibrin mesh — and fibrin failure bleeds into spaces: joints and muscles. The secondary factor 8 deficiency in severe von Willebrand disease can add a component of deep bleeding, which is why type 3 can look mixed.

LO 3 — Platelet disorders

Objective 3 · part 4

When the Platelet Itself Is Abnormal

Abbreviations in this section GPIb/IX/V glycoprotein Ib/IX/V — the receptor for von Willebrand factor, absent in Bernard–Soulier syndrome · GPIIb/IIIa glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, also called CD41/CD61 — the fibrinogen receptor, absent in Glanzmann thrombasthenia · ADP adenosine diphosphate · ATP adenosine triphosphate · Lumi-aggregometry a platelet study reading aggregation by light transmission and secretion by ATP luminescence · δ / α granules dense / alpha platelet granules · TXA2 thromboxane A2.

Rare, but conceptually clean: the same adhesion chain broken at the other end. The lecture puts both diseases on one diagram, and that pairing is the point.

🔑 Two diseases, one broken handshake

Recall the chain: collagen → von Willebrand factor → GPIb → platelet. Adhesion fails if you remove either partner in the handshake:

DiseaseWhat is missingSide of the handshake
von Willebrand diseaseVon Willebrand factor — the ligandThe plasma side
Bernard–Soulier syndromeGPIb/IX/V — the receptorThe platelet side

Both produce decreased adhesion and both bleed mucocutaneously. This is why the ristocetin cofactor assay uses normal fixed platelets — it deliberately removes the platelet side of the equation so the test reads the plasma side only.

🎙️ Two thirds of a clot's strength comes from platelets

A number worth carrying, because it converts Glanzmann thrombasthenia from a curiosity into something intuitive: roughly two thirds of the mechanical strength of a clot comes from the platelets enmeshed in it, not from the fibrin alone.

So in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where GPIIb/IIIa cannot bind fibrinogen and platelets therefore cannot be knitted into the mesh, the patient does form a fibrin clot — it is just mechanically weak, and it fails. Adhesion is intact (ristocetin normal); incorporation is not.

Also worth knowing what the aggregometer is actually detecting when it measures secretion: activated platelets change shape and release calcium, serotonin and ATP from their granules, and those released contents recruit further coagulation. The ATP is what the luciferase channel sees; the serotonin is what the serotonin release assay measures in the HIT workup in Part 2.

Platelet aggregation studies

  • Aggregation is assessed by change in light transmission — clumped platelets let more light through a stirred suspension.
  • Secretion is assessed by ATP-mediated luciferase activity — the firefly reaction, measuring ATP released from platelet dense granules. This is why the technique is called lumi-aggregometry: luminescence for secretion, transmission for aggregation, read together.
  • Platelet electron microscopy may be needed when a granule storage pool defect is suspected.

Slide 34 — Platelet aggregometry. Aggregation read as light transmission; secretion read as ATP luminescence.

🧠 How to read the platelet disorder table — look at the ristocetin column first

Ristocetin tests the GPIb–von Willebrand factor axis specifically. The other agonists — arachidonic acid, collagen, ADP — test activation and aggregation through other receptors. So:

  • Ristocetin low, everything else normal → the GPIb receptor is the problem → Bernard–Soulier syndrome (or von Willebrand disease, which the fixed-platelet design excludes).
  • Ristocetin normal, the others low → the receptor is fine but aggregation is broken → classically Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor).

Slide 35 — Platelet agonist responses. Read the ristocetin column first, then the pattern across the other agonists.

Platelet disorderATP release (thrombin)Arachidonic acidCollagenADPRistocetinThe defining note
Bernard–Soulier syndromeNormalNormalNormalNormalDecreasedGlycoprotein Ib-IX-V abnormality (interacts with von Willebrand factor). Smear shows thrombocytopenia with large platelets.
Glanzmann thrombastheniaNormalDecreasedDecreasedDecreasedNormalGlycoprotein IIb/IIIa abnormality (interacts with fibrinogen) — adhesion intact, aggregation fails.
Delta (δ) granule storage poolDecreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalElectron microscopy needed. Includes Hermansky–Pudlak and Chediak–Higashi.
Alpha (α) granule storage poolNormalVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalSmear shows gray platelets without typical granules — "gray platelet syndrome".
Arachidonic acid / thromboxane A2 pathwayNormalDecreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalAspirin produces identical findings — always ask about aspirin before diagnosing this.
Primary secretion defectsVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalSignal transduction problem — decreased granule release with a normal number of granules.
🎙️ Where platelet studies sit in the workup

Explicit sequencing advice: rule out hemophilia and von Willebrand disease first. Platelet function disorders are rare, and platelet aggregometry belongs in a second- or third-tier workup, not the initial panel.

The first-pass bleeding workup is therefore: PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count — plus von Willebrand testing, which has to be requested separately because the screen cannot find it.

🪝 Memory hook — B for Bernard, B for bind; G for Glanzmann, G for glue together

Bernard–Soulier cannot bind the vessel wall — GPIb is missing, so ristocetin fails. The "B" even appears in the receptor name. Glanzmann cannot glue platelets to each other — GPIIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen bridge, is missing, so everything except ristocetin fails. And Bernard–Soulier gives you a free extra clue on the smear: big platelets, low count.

Q: Aggregometry shows decreased response to arachidonic acid, collagen and ADP, with normal ristocetin and normal ATP release. Give two possible explanations and say how to separate them.

Answer

Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa deficiency) or an aspirin effect — the table notes explicitly that aspirin shows similar findings. Normal ristocetin rules out Bernard–Soulier and von Willebrand disease, because the GPIb axis is intact.

Separate them with the history first: recent aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug exposure. Then by pattern — a pure arachidonic acid / thromboxane defect (the aspirin pattern) tends to hit arachidonic acid hardest with only variable effects elsewhere, whereas Glanzmann abolishes aggregation to all of arachidonic acid, collagen and ADP. Definitive testing is flow cytometry for GPIIb/IIIa (CD41/CD61) expression. If aspirin is suspected, stop it and repeat after 7–10 days — aspirin is an irreversible inhibitor, so recovery requires new platelets.

LO 3 — Acquired causes

Objective 3 · part 5

Acquired Bleeding — Liver Disease, DIC, Vitamin K

The inherited disorders are the ones with names. The acquired ones are the ones you will actually meet on the wards, and they move both clotting times because they knock out several factors at once.

Abbreviations in this section DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · FDP fibrin degradation products · PCC prothrombin complex concentrate — a concentrated preparation of the vitamin K-dependent factors · FFP fresh frozen plasma.

Liver disease — a coagulopathy in both directions

🧠 Why liver disease is not simply "a bleeding state"

The liver makes almost all the coagulation proteins — the procoagulant factors and the natural anticoagulants protein C, protein S and antithrombin. Losing both sides at once produces a rebalanced but fragile hemostasis, which is why patients with end-stage liver disease can bleed and clot.

The practical consequence: a prolonged PT/INR in liver disease does not reliably predict bleeding the way it does in warfarin therapy, and it is not by itself a reason to transfuse plasma. The lecture cites the individualised-management literature for exactly this reason.

Slide 36 — Liver disease. Procoagulants and anticoagulants both fall, leaving a rebalanced but unstable system.

🎙️ Two practical notes on liver disease
  • Factor 8 is the exception that helps you. Because the liver makes every factor except von Willebrand factor and factor 8, factor 8 is typically normal or raised in liver disease but low in disseminated intravascular coagulation, where it is consumed with everything else. When the two are hard to separate, that is the discriminating assay.
  • The rebalancing does not protect them through surgery. The recording is blunt: these patients bleed a great deal intra-operatively, and it is routine for the blood bank to set aside 20–30 units for a liver transplant.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation

🔑 DIC is specification 3 failing — clotting that is not localised

Go back to the orientation: the system must respond to injury quickly and in a localised fashion. In DIC, coagulation is triggered systemically. Widespread microvascular thrombosis consumes platelets and factors, and simultaneously drives fibrinolysis. The patient therefore clots and bleeds at the same time — the defining paradox.

TestDirection in DICWhy
Platelet countFallsConsumed in microthrombi
PT and aPTTBoth prolongedFactors consumed — and a common-pathway and fibrinogen deficit hits both tests
FibrinogenFallsConsumed converting to fibrin. A falling trend is more useful than a single value, since fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant and starts high in sepsis
D-dimer / FDPRise, often markedlyActive fibrin formation and breakdown
SmearSchistocytesRed cells sheared on intravascular fibrin strands — a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

Slide 37 — DIC. Systemic activation, consumption of factors and platelets, and secondary fibrinolysis.

Slide 38 — DIC: causes, signs and management. The underlying trigger is the treatment target.

⚠️ The management principle for DIC

Treat the underlying cause. DIC is always secondary — to sepsis, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe, major trauma. Product support (platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate) is given for bleeding or before a procedure, not to correct a number on a panel. DIC also reappears in the Complete Blood Count lecture as one of the causes of schistocytes on a smear, and in Part 2 alongside the thrombotic microangiopathies it must be distinguished from.

Vitamin K deficiency and acquired inhibitors

🔑 Vitamin K — factors 2, 7, 9, 10 (and proteins C and S)

Vitamin K is required to make factors 2, 7, 9 and 10 functional, plus the anticoagulants protein C and protein S. Deficiency can follow malnutrition, malabsorption, or prolonged antibiotics.

Vitamin K injection is part of standard neonatal care — newborns are relatively deficient (little placental transfer, low stores, sterile gut), and without it they are at risk of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, including intracranial hemorrhage.

Because factor 7 has the shortest half-life of the four, the PT prolongs first, and an isolated long PT with a normal aPTT is the classic early picture. This is the same mechanism warfarin exploits, covered in Part 2.

🎙️ Factor 5 — how to tell vitamin K deficiency from liver disease

Both prolong the PT. Both eventually prolong the aPTT. The clean discriminator is a factor the slides do not mention:

Factors 2, 7, 9, 10Factor 5Why
Vitamin K deficiency (or warfarin)LowNormalFactor 5 is not vitamin K dependent, so it is untouched
Liver diseaseLowAlso lowThe liver makes factor 5 too, so synthetic failure takes it down as well

Low 2, 7, 9, 10 with a normal factor 5 = vitamin K deficiency. Everything low including factor 5 = liver disease. A further practical point from the recording: babies born outside a hospital may miss the routine neonatal vitamin K injection, so ask about the birth setting.

🧠 Acquired factor inhibitors and acquired von Willebrand disease
  • Associated with autoimmune disorders, malignancy, and cardiac valvular disease.
  • The typical patient is older, presenting with a new bleeding diathesis and no lifelong bleeding history — that contrast with a congenital disorder is the diagnostic clue.
  • The mixing study is the discriminator: an acquired inhibitor fails to correct.
  • Acquired von Willebrand disease with aortic stenosis is worth knowing as a mechanism — shear stress across the stenotic valve unfolds von Willebrand factor and exposes it to ADAMTS13, stripping out the high molecular weight multimers. It produces a type-2-like picture in a patient with a murmur and gastrointestinal bleeding (Heyde syndrome).
🎙️ The acquired inhibitor patient, and how they are treated

The recording sharpens the clinical picture: these patients look exactly like hemophilia or von Willebrand disease, except they have no history — the diathesis appears suddenly, often in their 50s. For some reason they have started making antibodies against factor 8.

Management has two halves: treat the bleeding as you would in hemophilia (bypassing agents, since infused factor is neutralised), and suppress the antibody with immunosuppressants — the second half being what distinguishes acquired from congenital disease, because here the antibody can actually be eradicated.

Q: A septic patient in the intensive care unit has a falling platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, fibrinogen dropping from 480 to 140 mg/dL over two days, a markedly raised D-dimer, and schistocytes on the smear. What is the diagnosis, and what is the most important treatment?

Answer

Disseminated intravascular coagulation, secondary to sepsis. Every leg is present: consumption (falling platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged clotting times), fibrinolysis (high D-dimer) and microangiopathy (schistocytes).

Note that the fibrinogen at 140 is still within many reference ranges — the downward trend from 480 is the finding, because fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant and should be high in sepsis.

The most important treatment is aggressive treatment of the sepsis. Blood products are given for bleeding or before procedures, not to normalise numbers.

Q: A 74-year-old with no prior bleeding history develops large spontaneous hematomas. aPTT is prolonged, PT normal, platelet count normal. A 1:1 mix does not correct. What is going on?

Answer

An acquired factor inhibitor — most commonly an acquired factor 8 inhibitor (acquired hemophilia A). Three features point there: an isolated prolonged aPTT (intrinsic pathway), a mixing study that fails to correct (inhibitor rather than deficiency), and above all a new bleeding diathesis in an older patient — a congenital factor deficiency would have declared itself decades earlier.

Look for an underlying autoimmune disorder or malignancy. Confirm with a factor 8 activity level and a Bethesda titre.

Q: Two patients each have a prolonged PT. Patient A has factors 2, 7, 9 and 10 all low with a normal factor 5. Patient B has factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and 5 all low. What distinguishes them?

Answer

Patient A has vitamin K deficiency (or is on warfarin). Patient B has liver disease.

Factor 5 is not vitamin K dependent. Vitamin K is required only for factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and proteins C and S — so a pure vitamin K problem leaves factor 5 untouched. The liver, by contrast, synthesises factor 5 as well, so hepatic synthetic failure drags it down with everything else.

Low 2, 7, 9, 10 with a normal factor 5 = vitamin K. Everything low including 5 = liver. A supporting check runs the other way: factor 8 is normal or high in liver disease (it is not made by hepatocytes) but low in disseminated intravascular coagulation.

For patient A, ask about nutrition, malabsorption, prolonged antibiotics — and in a neonate, whether the birth happened outside a hospital, where the routine vitamin K injection may have been missed.

🩺 Lecture summary — the closing slide
  • There is a wide range of bleeding disorders.
  • Evaluate with PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count, and von Willebrand testing — note that von Willebrand testing is listed separately, because the first four will not find it.
  • Factor deficiency; von Willebrand disease (challenging because of the variety of subtypes); dysfibrinogenemia (which can also cause clotting); platelet disorders (rare).
  • Proper coagulation also depends on blood vessels and endothelium — the panel can be normal and the patient can still bleed.

Glossary and Abbreviations

Every abbreviation and technical term used in this file, written out and defined.

Tests and laboratory terms
PT — prothrombin time
Clotting time measuring the extrinsic and common pathways. Most sensitive to factor 7. Normal roughly 12–15 seconds.
INR — international normalised ratio
A mathematically standardised PT, so that a result from one laboratory means the same as a result from another. The number warfarin therapy is dosed against.
aPTT — activated partial thromboplastin time
Clotting time measuring the intrinsic and common pathways. Most sensitive to factors 8, 9, 11, 12. Normal roughly 25–39 seconds.
TT — thrombin time
Time to clot after adding thrombin directly; tests the final fibrinogen-to-fibrin step. Normal roughly 10–20 seconds.
Mixing study
Patient plasma mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma and the clotting time repeated. Corrects → factor deficiency. Fails to correct → inhibitor.
D-dimer
A fragment released when cross-linked fibrin is degraded by plasmin. Raised whenever a clot is being formed and broken down.
FDP — fibrin degradation products
The broader family of fragments released by fibrinolysis; D-dimer is the specific, commonly measured one.
Thromboelastography (TEG) / thromboelastometry (ROTEM)
Viscoelastic whole-blood tests that watch clot initiation, strengthening and lysis in real time — they monitor all phases of clot development rather than a single endpoint.
Ristocetin cofactor assay (VWF:RCo)
Measures von Willebrand factor function. Ristocetin forces von Willebrand factor to bind GPIb on normal fixed platelets; the resulting agglutination is read as increased light transmission.
VWF:Ag — von Willebrand factor antigen
Measures how much von Willebrand factor protein is present, regardless of whether it works.
Multimer analysis
Western blot separating von Willebrand factor multimers by size. Used to identify loss of high molecular weight multimers in type 2 disease.
Lumi-aggregometry
Platelet study reading aggregation as light transmission and granule secretion as ATP-driven luciferase luminescence, simultaneously.
Sodium citrate tube
The light-blue-top tube for coagulation testing. Citrate reversibly binds calcium; the 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio must be exact or clotting times are falsely prolonged.
EDTA — ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
The anticoagulant in the lavender-top tube used for the complete blood count. Binds calcium irreversibly, so it cannot be used for clotting times.
Cascade components
Procoagulant
A protein that promotes clot formation — the numbered factors, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, tissue factor, calcium, phospholipid.
Anticoagulant (natural)
A protein that restrains clot formation — protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, plasmin, tissue plasminogen activator, and the heparans on intact endothelium.
Intrinsic pathway
Contact-activated arm: factors 12 → 11 → 9 → 8. Measured by the aPTT.
Extrinsic pathway
Tissue-factor-activated arm: factor 7. Measured by the PT.
Common pathway
The shared trunk: factors 10 → 5 → 2 (prothrombin → thrombin), then fibrinogen → fibrin. A defect here prolongs both tests.
Fibrinogen (factor 1)
The soluble plasma protein that thrombin cleaves into insoluble fibrin, the structural polymer of a clot.
Tissue factor (factor 3, TF)
Membrane protein exposed by vessel injury; the physiological trigger of coagulation, acting through factor 7.
Thrombin (factor 2a, FIIa)
The central enzyme. Converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and feeds back to activate factors 5, 8, 11 and 13, amplifying its own generation.
Factor 13
Cross-links fibrin to stabilise the finished clot. Deficiency causes delayed bleeding with a normal PT and aPTT.
VWF — von Willebrand factor
Large multimeric glycoprotein from endothelial cells (Weibel–Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes. Two jobs: platelet adhesion via GPIb, and carrier for factor 8.
HMWM — high molecular weight multimers
The largest von Willebrand factor forms, which carry most of its hemostatic activity. Trimmed by ADAMTS13.
ADAMTS13
The protease that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers down to size. Its deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (Part 2).
Weibel–Palade body
Storage granule inside an endothelial cell holding von Willebrand factor, released on stimulation — the store that desmopressin mobilises.
Fibrinolysis
Breakdown of the clot once healing is complete. tPA converts plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin.
tPA — tissue plasminogen activator
The endogenous activator of plasminogen; also a therapeutic thrombolytic drug.
Antiplasmin
The natural inhibitor of plasmin. Deficiency allows premature clot lysis, causing delayed bleeding.
Platelet terms
Primary hemostasis
Formation of the platelet plug — adhesion, activation, aggregation. Failure bleeds mucocutaneously.
Secondary hemostasis
Formation of the fibrin mesh that reinforces the plug. Failure bleeds into joints and muscles.
GPIb/IX/V — glycoprotein Ib/IX/V
The platelet receptor that binds von Willebrand factor, mediating adhesion. Absent in Bernard–Soulier syndrome.
GPIIb/IIIa — glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (CD41/CD61)
The platelet receptor that binds fibrinogen, mediating aggregation between platelets. Absent in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
Bernard–Soulier syndrome
Deficiency of GPIb/IX/V. Decreased ristocetin response, with large platelets and thrombocytopenia on the smear.
Glanzmann thrombasthenia
Deficiency of GPIIb/IIIa. Decreased aggregation to arachidonic acid, collagen and ADP, with normal ristocetin.
Storage pool disease
Deficiency of platelet granules — delta (dense) granules, as in Hermansky–Pudlak and Chediak–Higashi, or alpha granules, giving "gray platelets".
Petechiae
Pinpoint non-blanching skin haemorrhages, typical of platelet problems.
Ecchymosis
A bruise. Small and superficial in platelet disorders; large and deep in coagulation factor disorders.
Hemarthrosis
Bleeding into a joint — the signature of secondary hemostatic failure, classically hemophilia.
Diseases and drugs
Hemophilia A
Factor 8 deficiency. X-linked, 1 in 5,000 males.
Hemophilia B (Christmas disease)
Factor 9 deficiency. X-linked, 1 in 30,000 males.
Inhibitor
An antibody that neutralises a coagulation factor. In hemophilia it is an alloantibody against infused factor; in acquired hemophilia it is an autoantibody.
Emicizumab (Hemlibra)
A bispecific antibody bridging factor 9a and factor 10, reproducing factor 8a's cofactor function. A bypassing agent, effective despite anti-factor-8 inhibitors.
VWD — von Willebrand disease
The most common inherited bleeding disorder. Type 1 partial quantitative deficiency; type 2 qualitative defect; type 3 near-complete absence.
DDAVP — desmopressin
A vasopressin analogue that releases stored von Willebrand factor from endothelium. First-line in type 1; potentially harmful in type 2B.
Humate P, Alphanate, Wilate, Vonvendi
Von Willebrand factor-containing concentrates. The first two are plasma-derived factor 8 / von Willebrand factor products; Wilate is plasma-derived von Willebrand factor; Vonvendi is recombinant.
Cryoprecipitate
A plasma fraction rich in fibrinogen, factor 8, von Willebrand factor and factor 13. Avoided in von Willebrand disease now that virally-inactivated concentrates exist.
DIC — disseminated intravascular coagulation
Systemic, non-localised coagulation activation causing simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding. Low platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, falling fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes.
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
Inherited malformation of small vessels causing recurrent bleeding despite a normal coagulation system.
Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon
A fast-growing vascular tumour that traps and consumes platelets, causing thrombocytopenia and bleeding.
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Inherited connective tissue disorder; bleeding results from inadequate vessel wall support, with normal clotting tests.
Paraprotein
An abnormal monoclonal immunoglobulin that can interfere with platelet function and fibrin polymerisation, causing bleeding.
Vitamin K
Required for functional factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and proteins C and S. Given routinely to newborns; deficiency prolongs the PT first because factor 7 has the shortest half-life.
PCC — prothrombin complex concentrate
A concentrate of the vitamin K-dependent factors, used to reverse warfarin or replace those factors rapidly.
Dysfibrinogenemia
Fibrinogen present in normal amount but structurally abnormal. Can cause either bleeding or clotting.

🎯 Coagulation I — High-Yield One-Pager

Cyril Jacquot, MD, PhD · condensed by learning objective — LO1 cascade components · LO2 pathways and their tests · LO3 distinguishing bleeding disorders

LO 1 · CASCADE

Four system specifications

  • Balance bleeding vs clotting protection
  • Maintain hemostasis and vessel patency
  • Respond fast and locally — failure = DIC
  • Return to baseline — fibrinolysis

Three ingredients

  • Platelets (number + function)
  • Fibrin clot (production + breakdown)
  • Blood vessels / endothelium — normal panel ≠ no bleeding disorder

Procoagulants

  • Factors 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13
  • Fibrinogen = factor 1 · Tissue factor = factor 3 · Calcium = "factor 4"
  • VWF · Phospholipid (platelet surface)

Natural anticoagulants

  • Protein C + protein S → inactivate factors 5a, 8a
  • Antithrombin III → the target heparin works through
  • Plasmin, tPA
  • Intact endothelium — expresses heparans

Pathway map

  • Intrinsic 12→11→9→8 → aPTT
  • 3=tissue factor · 4=calcium · 6 retired
  • Liver makes all except VWF + factor 8
  • Extrinsic 7 → PT
  • Common 10→5→2→fibrinogen → both
  • Thrombin feeds back on 5, 8, 11, 13
  • 13 cross-links fibrin (invisible to PT/aPTT)
LO 2 · TESTS

Collection tube

  • Sodium citrate (light blue), reversible calcium binding
  • 9:1 blood:citrate is critical
  • Underfilled → falsely prolonged → rejected

The 50% rule

  • ~50% is where aPTT starts to prolong (PT ~55%)
  • 30–40% still hemostatically fine
  • <20% → aPTT >45 sec = hemophilia; severe >100 sec
  • Range = 95% CI → ~5% of healthy people fall outside

Mixing study

  • Corrects → factor deficiency
  • Fails to correct → inhibitor (acquired factor antibody, lupus anticoagulant)
  • Incubate 30–60 min @37°C to catch a slow factor 8 inhibitor
  • Test is run on plasma → platelets spun out → blind to them

⚠ The blind spot

  • VWD and platelet disorders do NOT prolong PT or aPTT
  • Factor 12 deficiency prolongs aPTT but causes no bleeding
  • Factor 13 deficiency: normal PT/aPTT, delayed bleeding

Bleeding pattern → disease

  • Mucocutaneous (nose, gums, menorrhagia, petechiae) → VWD / platelets
  • Joint + muscle (hemarthrosis, deep hematoma) → hemophilia
  • Delayed → factor 13 or antiplasmin
LO 3 · DISORDERS

Hemophilia

  • A = factor 8, 1:5,000 males · B = factor 9, 1:30,000 males
  • C = factor 11, autosomal, milder, post-surgical
  • Both X-linked; long aPTT, normal PT, mix corrects
  • Severity: <1% severe · 1–5% moderate · >5–30% mild; treat to ~20–30%
  • Inhibitors are the main problem → emicizumab (bridges 9a–10)

von Willebrand disease

  • Most common inherited bleeding disorder; autosomal dominant; ~1:8,000 symptomatic
  • Activity ≈ antigen → quantitative: type 1 (<30%), type 3 (<3%)
  • Activity << antigen (ratio <0.5–0.7) → qualitative: type 2, abnormal multimers
  • Low VWF 30–50% = VWD only if bleeding history · group O runs lower
  • Rx: type 1 DDAVP; 2B/3 Humate P / Alphanate; avoid cryoprecipitate

Platelet: the broken handshake

  • Chain: collagen → VWF → GPIb → platelet
  • VWD = ligand missing · Bernard–Soulier = GPIb receptor missing
  • Ristocetin low only → Bernard–Soulier (large platelets, low count)
  • Ristocetin normal, rest low → Glanzmann (GPIIb/IIIa) — or aspirin

Acquired

  • DIC: ↓platelets, ↑PT and aPTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑↑D-dimer, schistocytes → treat the cause
  • Liver: loses pro- and anticoagulants → rebalanced; INR does not predict bleeding
  • Vitamin K: factors 2, 7, 9, 10 + proteins C/S; PT prolongs first; routine in neonates
  • Factor 5 normal → vitamin K; factor 5 low → liver
  • Acquired inhibitor: older patient, new diathesis, mix fails to correct
